routes.description: Establish secular humanism as more adept at advancing human flourishing through evidence-sensitive, revisable methods and practical comparison with Christian guidance.
routes.successCriteria: Show that human flourishing is the relevant shared goal and that secular methods yield more reliable decisions, moral guidance, learning, and conflict resolution than Christian methods.

motionBridge.description: Secular humanism is more adept than Christianity at achieving the motion's practical goals.

centralBridges.description: Relative evidence about shared human interests permits meaningful comparison without an ultimate standard.
Evidence-sensitive and revisable inquiry produces transferable knowledge and improved practical outcomes.
Autonomy, equality, consequences, and human interests provide better moral guidance than scriptural authority.
Public evidence resolves disagreement more reliably than competing claims of revelation or interpretation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Using shared logical axioms does not require adding an unsupported divine explanation.
The capacity to revise goals and methods in light of outcomes improves error correction.

routes.description: Defeat the claimed superiority by arguing that secular humanism lacks non-arbitrary foundations for rational inference, science, and ethics while Christianity supplies them.
routes.successCriteria: Show that secular humanism cannot justify the standards and cognitive tools its comparison requires, and that Christian revelation and God's character provide a coherent superior foundation.

motionBridge.description: Secular humanism cannot be superior because its foundational commitments undermine its own claims.

centralBridges.description: A valid superiority comparison requires a non-arbitrary standard applicable across both worldviews.
Naturalistic physical processes cannot adequately justify trustworthy logical inference.
Secular humanism cannot justify the logical and inductive presuppositions required by science.
Consequentialist human-flourishing ethics lacks an objective standard and becomes circular or permissive.

subsidiaryBridges.description: God's invariant character and revelation ground logic, natural regularity, and moral norms.
Christian disagreements over nonessentials do not defeat shared essential doctrines or New Testament ethics.

sections.title: The standard for superiority
sections.rationale: The parties contest whether relative facts about a shared goal suffice or whether comparison requires a worldview-neutral objective foundation.

proMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
proMoves.proposition: Reasonably warranted beliefs and non-subjective facts permit relative comparisons of methods without absolute certainty or an ultimate measuring standard.

sourceSpan.excerpt: absolute certainty isn't relevant to this discussion... the facts of reality, which... are non-subjective and universal, can dictate which methods are superior. Relative comparisons are all that is needed.

proMoves.attributionBasis: The span occurs continuously within Dillahunty's identified opening statement before Slick is introduced.

response.rationale: This is an opening constructive criterion for comparison and therefore has no earlier selected target or response component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim distinguishes reasonable warrant and relative comparison from absolute certainty and expressly limits its required standard.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparative claim is presented without certainty and includes explicit acknowledgment of fallibility and reasonable warrant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from shared facts and a stipulated goal to relative comparison is stable, with only the choice of evaluative indicators left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The general comparative examples support the warrant, though no detailed measurement framework for flourishing is supplied here.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive, it directly establishes the standard that the affirmative case will use throughout the debate.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the declared central bridge concerning a workable comparative standard.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops Dillahunty's own criterion without relying on a reconstruction of a live opposing position.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: The opening expressly rejects a demand for absolute certainty and argues that universal facts and relative performance can establish superiority.

conMoves.speaker: Matt Slick
conMoves.proposition: A worldview that is self-refuting cannot be superior, so secular humanism must first provide coherent foundations for knowledge and rationality.

sourceSpan.excerpt: one philosophical position cannot be superior to another... if that philosophical position is self-refuting... that which is self-refuting is automatically inferior to that which is not self-refuting.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span occurs in Slick's formally introduced opening and follows his explicit statement of his governing criterion.

components.text: Relative comparison is sufficient without an ultimate foundation.

response.rationale: Slick directly rejects the sufficiency of the pro criterion and states the defeating consequence: a self-refuting worldview is necessarily inferior regardless of its preferred metric.

precisionFindings.rationale: The criterion is clear, but 'self-refuting' expands toward any alleged inability to account for foundational knowledge without a fully defended scope condition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Actual self-refutation would defeat superiority, but the move treats an accounting gap as sufficient before establishing that it is a contradiction.

charity.alternative: Dillahunty's position requires only comparative performance relative to a shared practical goal.
charity.decisiveQualification: The affirmative does not claim absolute certainty or a complete ultimate account of every presupposition.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional criterion is intelligible, but it compresses the bridge from lack of ultimate accounting to genuine self-refutation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move states a philosophical test but has not yet demonstrated that secular humanism actually satisfies the antecedent.

responsiveness.rationale: It directly diagnoses the alleged inadequacy of relative comparison and expressly states why that defect would defeat superiority.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con route's central requirement for a non-arbitrary comparative standard.

representationalCharity.rationale: It recognizes the comparative project but understates Dillahunty's explicit distinction between reasonable warrant and absolute foundations.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Slick repeatedly states that self-refutation makes a worldview inferior and uses that proposition to replace the pro comparative test with a foundational one.

sections.title: Empirical method, learning, and science
sections.rationale: The core practical comparison pits secular humanism's revisable empirical learning against the objection that science cannot justify its own logical and inductive presuppositions.

proMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
proMoves.proposition: Secular humanism improves flourishing by testing outcomes, learning transferable methods, and revising its goals and practices when evidence changes.

sourceSpan.excerpt: medical treatments... foster a better understanding and lead to improvements in human flourishing... the secular process is better because we learn more from it... It is revisible. It can change its positions and it can change its goals.

proMoves.attributionBasis: The passage is a continuous portion of Dillahunty's opening, using his medical-treatment example and stated secular-humanist goals.

response.rationale: This constructive presents the affirmative method-and-results route before any selected con response and therefore has no response targets.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly identifies learning, practical outcomes, and revisability, while acknowledging that secular humanism lacks complete answers.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The practical methodological advantage is plausible and qualified, though 'by definition' briefly states more than the illustrative evidence establishes.

charity.alternative: A religious practice might sometimes produce a beneficial result, including recovery following prayer.
charity.decisiveQualification: A beneficial result alone does not supply a reliable mechanism or transferable understanding.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The route from testing and causal understanding to reusable knowledge and improved future decisions is coherent and explicitly developed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Medical treatment, prayer, and institutional learning are apt examples, though broad claims about all flourishing outcomes remain incompletely documented.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive it substantially develops the central affirmative method rather than merely asserting a preferred conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central empirical-method bridge with method, mechanism, and outcome comparisons.

representationalCharity.rationale: It grants for argument's sake that prayer could work and then identifies the narrower deficiency of nontransferable explanation.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: The selected span combines the strongest medical-method comparison with the later explicit claims that humanist principles are outcome-tested and revisable.

conMoves.speaker: Matt Slick
conMoves.proposition: Secular reliance on science cannot justify the laws of logic or uniformity of nature that scientific inference itself presupposes, whereas Christianity can ground them in God.

sourceSpan.excerpt: the scientific method is based on philosophical assumptions... assumes the validity of the laws of logic... science presupposes the regularity of nature... Christianity... can trust that the universe is made in a consistent and predictable manner.

conMoves.attributionBasis: This is a continuous subsection of Slick's opening explicitly introduced as his treatment of science.

components.text: Outcome testing and revisability improve practical knowledge and flourishing.

response.rationale: The move supplies contrary material about science's ultimate presuppositions but does not contact the target's empirical claim that revisable methods yield transferable practical learning.

precisionFindings.rationale: The regress challenge is recoverable, but the scope shifts between science, methodological naturalism, and the full secular-humanist worldview.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The inability to non-circularly prove induction does not by itself establish that secular science is unusable or that Christian premises uniquely justify it.

charity.alternative: Dillahunty offers fallible, outcome-sensitive science as a practical method rather than a self-validating source of certainty.
charity.decisiveQualification: The affirmative expressly disclaims absolute certainty and compares demonstrated performance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regress problem is intelligible, but the move treats inability to prove presuppositions scientifically as a defeater of practical scientific warrant.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The philosophical observations about logic and induction are relevant, while the exclusive Christian solution is principally asserted through scripture.

responsiveness.rationale: It bears on the reliability of secular inquiry but does not answer the target's concrete learning, revision, and outcome comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the declared central con bridge challenging secular justification of science.

representationalCharity.rationale: It largely recasts practical methodological reliance as a claim that science can validate its own ultimate presuppositions.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Slick separately develops the dependence of science on logic and induction, then contrasts those assumptions with a scriptural account of divine consistency.

sections.title: Moral standards and practical guidance
sections.rationale: The ethical dispute concerns whether autonomy, equality, harm, and consequences provide corrigible guidance or collapse into an arbitrary circular standard.

proMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
proMoves.proposition: Starting from equality, autonomy, cooperation, and flourishing rules out slavery and murder while supplying practical reasons for peaceful conduct.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Isn't it enough to work for peace in the life that we have now?... when you begin with a foundation of equality and autonomy... Slavery and murder are done from the outset... We talked about equality.

proMoves.attributionBasis: The material is part of Dillahunty's uninterrupted opening comparison of secular and biblical ethical guidance.

response.rationale: The move constructively states the secular ethical route and its practical consequences without responding to an earlier selected con move.

precisionFindings.rationale: The practical principles are clear, though the categorical claim that they rule out all slavery or killing lacks explicit conflict conditions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Equality and autonomy strongly oppose slavery, but the categorical formulation compresses difficult cases involving competing harms or autonomy.

charity.alternative: Christian scripture contains morally useful commands and reasons to pursue peace.
charity.decisiveQualification: Useful biblical material does not establish Christianity as its unique source or remove contrary scriptural material.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from equality and autonomy to opposition to enslavement is strong, though the move compresses how multiple principles resolve hard conflicts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The principles and biblical contrasts are relevant but broad historical and textual claims are offered without detailed representative support in this span.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive, it directly supplies moral principles and practical applications central to the affirmative comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially advances the pro central bridge concerning secular ethical guidance.

representationalCharity.rationale: It concedes that Christianity contains good advice while denying that isolated advice establishes comparative superiority.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty contrasts practical reasons for peace and cooperation with divine approval, then applies equality and autonomy to slavery and murder.

conMoves.speaker: Matt Slick
conMoves.proposition: Consequentialist ethics cannot non-circularly establish that reducing harm is good and may fail to condemn intrinsically wrongful acts when no detectable harm occurs.

sourceSpan.excerpt: secular humanists hold that ethics is consequential to be judged by results... How do we know that the reduction of harm is good?... You have to appeal to the very act that is wrong by nature, and that refutes consequentialism.

conMoves.attributionBasis: Slick explicitly introduces ethics in his opening and develops this challenge continuously in his own speaking turn.

components.text: Equality, autonomy, and flourishing supply sufficient reasons to prohibit slavery and serious wrongdoing.
Christian commands do not uniquely source good guidance and coexist with contrary scriptural material.

response.rationale: Slick attacks the sufficiency of harm and consequence standards but does not answer the target's textual and comparative challenge concerning Christian guidance.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge is clear, but it moves between consequentialism, harm reduction, subjectivity, and Dillahunty's plural principles as though they were identical.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The hypothetical exposes a possible insufficiency in a simple harm test, but it does not refute every plural or rule-consequentialist account.

charity.alternative: Dillahunty's ethical case uses equality, autonomy, cooperation, likely consequences, and revisable evidence rather than harm alone.
charity.decisiveQualification: The pro account is plural and can treat rights violations and social effects as consequences or independent constraints.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The challenge to a bare harm criterion is coherent, but the conclusion generalizes from that narrow criterion to consequentialism as a whole.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The coma hypothetical tests one formulation effectively, yet the move supplies little defense of intrinsic wrongness or the claimed exhaustive dilemma.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive sufficiency of secular moral standards while leaving the comparative biblical component unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con central bridge challenging the foundation of secular morality.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument reduces Dillahunty's broader, revisable ethical framework to a single immediate-harm criterion.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: The span contains Slick's complete circularity objection and the no-detectable-harm hypothetical used to argue that consequences require an independent norm.

sections.title: Revelation, disagreement, and Christian guidance
sections.rationale: The parties dispute whether Christian interpretive disagreement disables practical guidance or concerns only nonessential details within a stable revealed framework.

proMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
proMoves.proposition: Expert Christians can use the same scriptures to support incompatible salvation accounts, showing that revelation lacks a reliable conflict-resolution method.

sourceSpan.excerpt: two people who both believe they're Christians are pointing to the same book... confirm mutually exclusive contradictory positions... They both think they have a method to reach the truth and they reach mutually exclusive contradictory positions.

proMoves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty develops the example in his opening and explicitly identifies Slick and Jesse Morrell as the disputants.

response.rationale: This is the opening affirmative example for the conflict-resolution issue and does not respond to an earlier selected con move.

precisionFindings.rationale: The example and claimed methodological consequence are clear, and Dillahunty expressly allows possible misremembering, though he extrapolates from one debate.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The case supports an interpretive-reliability concern, but one disagreement cannot alone establish Christianity's general inability to resolve conflicts.

charity.alternative: The Christian debaters may share the essential doctrine of salvation while disputing only its order or mechanics.
charity.decisiveQualification: The disputed order may still matter to the claimed method of determining what one must do to be saved.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from incompatible expert readings to a reliability problem is sound, with a remaining bridge from one case to the system generally.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A specific debate supplies relevant evidence, but the transcript does not independently establish the representativeness or precise doctrinal stakes.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive, it directly develops the pro route concerning disagreement and conflict resolution.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the declared central conflict-resolution bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It acknowledges both Christians' expertise and shared salvation goal, though it gives limited attention to the essential/nonessential distinction.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty describes mutually incompatible scriptural cases offered by two Christian apologists and identifies the resulting methodological problem.

conMoves.speaker: Matt Slick
conMoves.proposition: The disputed salvation order is nonessential because both Christians affirm salvation by grace through faith in Christ, while current Christian ethics is codified in New Testament revelation.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Jesse Morrell and I both believe that salvation is by grace alone, through faith alone, and Christ alone... the differences of our opinions are... non-essential... Christian principles today, found in the New Testament.

conMoves.attributionBasis: Slick explicitly names himself and Morrell and answers Dillahunty's opening example within Slick's uninterrupted opening statement.

components.text: The incompatible salvation interpretations concern a methodologically decisive question.
Revelation lacks a reliable procedure for resolving the competing interpretations.

response.rationale: Slick narrows the significance of the disagreement by identifying shared essentials, but he does not provide a procedure that resolves the incompatible readings.

precisionFindings.rationale: The essential/nonessential distinction is clear, although the criterion for classifying the disputed order as nonessential remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Shared doctrinal essentials weaken the example, but merely labeling the remaining disagreement adiaphora does not resolve its epistemic significance.

charity.alternative: Dillahunty argues that disagreement over salvation's process tests Christianity's ability to derive crucial guidance from scripture.
charity.decisiveQualification: His criticism concerns reliability of interpretation, not merely whether the debaters share a broad creed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between essential agreement and secondary ordering is coherent, but its consequence for interpretive reliability is underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Slick specifies the shared doctrine and disputed order but principally asserts their relative importance from within his theological framework.

responsiveness.rationale: The answer contacts the importance of the contradiction but leaves the decisive conflict-resolution mechanism unaddressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move supports the declared subsidiary bridge concerning scriptural coherence and therefore remains within the subsidiary band.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately identifies Dillahunty's example and supplies a meaningful qualification, though it narrows the challenge more than the pro argument permits.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Slick directly answers the Morrell example by identifying their common soteriological commitments, disputed order, and his New Testament ethical source.

sections.title: Naturalistic reason and divine grounding
sections.rationale: The most sustained exchange asks whether physical cognition is self-defeating and whether adding God explains logic better than shared axiomatic presuppositions.

proMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
proMoves.proposition: Secular humanism may presuppose logic without self-refutation because both sides share those axioms, while the further claim that God accounts for them remains undemonstrated.

sourceSpan.excerpt: secular humanism doesn't claim that it can account for the laws of logic. So it's not self-refuting... presuppositionalists... never demonstrate... my worldview accounts for this because God... we agree on the foundations of logic.

proMoves.attributionBasis: The answer is delivered in Dillahunty's distinctive first-person framing during audience questioning and directly contrasts his view with Slick's.

components.text: Physical causation makes trustworthy logical inference unavailable.
Christian theism supplies a demonstrated account unavailable to naturalism.

response.rationale: Dillahunty answers both the alleged self-refutation and the comparative Christian advantage by distinguishing an admitted axiom from contradiction and challenging the unsupported divine step.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move carefully distinguishes presupposing logic, accounting for logic, demonstrating usefulness, and adding a divine explanation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Dillahunty openly concedes that he lacks an ultimate account and limits his conclusion to the absence of a demonstrated Christian advantage.

charity.alternative: Slick argues that a transcendent divine mind uniquely grounds universal logical laws and trustworthy cognition.
charity.decisiveQualification: The Christian claim is intended as an explanatory account, not merely an additional arbitrary premise.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between using a shared axiom and claiming an exclusive further explanation directly blocks the asserted contradiction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The shared commitment to logic and lack of a demonstrated inferential path from logic to God strongly support the limited rebuttal.

responsiveness.rationale: The move explicitly contacts both decisive components of the naturalistic self-refutation argument and the claimed Christian alternative.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move supports the declared subsidiary bridge concerning logical presupposition and remains within that tier's band.

representationalCharity.rationale: It presents the presuppositionalist claim in its stronger unique-grounding form before arguing that the crucial demonstrations are absent.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: The selected answer concedes the secular stopping point, invokes shared logical axioms, and challenges both uniqueness and demonstration in the theistic account.

conMoves.speaker: Matt Slick
conMoves.proposition: If cognition consists only of physical chemical reactions, secular humanism cannot justify trusting its logical conclusions and therefore undermines belief in itself.

sourceSpan.excerpt: it's still a set of chemicals... how do you justify... that your logical inferences in your brain could be trusted?... you couldn't even know if secular humanism is true... It refutes itself.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The passage is a continuous part of Slick's opening and repeatedly contrasts the naturalistic brain with his Christian account.

components.text: Evidence-sensitive human cognition can reliably test, revise, and improve methods.

response.rationale: Slick directly attacks the reliability presupposed by the empirical method and explicitly claims the defect makes secular humanism self-refuting.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument is recoverable, but it moves from physical implementation to 'just chemicals' and from Dillahunty's methodological naturalism to exhaustive philosophical naturalism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move declares self-refutation without establishing that causally realized cognition cannot track truth or that secular humanism entails the asserted exhaustive reduction.

charity.alternative: Complex physical cognitive systems can be fallible yet truth-tracking through perception, correction, and intersubjective testing.
charity.decisiveQualification: Dillahunty's stated view is methodological rather than a demonstrated commitment to exhaustive ontological reduction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument depends on an unsupported inference from chemical realization to inability to track truth and equivocates between causal production and rational justification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The vinegar analogy and repeated assertion do not substantiate the claim that complex neural systems cannot implement valid inference.

responsiveness.rationale: It directly attacks the reliability required by the selected secular method and clearly states the alleged defeating consequence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central con bridge challenging naturalistic rationality.

representationalCharity.rationale: It treats methodological naturalism as exhaustive reductive naturalism and omits the opponent's fallibilist, intersubjective account of correction.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Slick's strongest opening formulation links physical causation to untrustworthy inference and expressly concludes that secular humanism is self-refuting.

con.rationale: No distinct debate-wide consequence remains outside the selected foundational objections, their replies, ratings, and weighted issue structure.

eligibility.completionCriterion: Defeat secular superiority by establishing foundational insufficiency and a coherent Christian alternative.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: No independently unscored consequence was identified.
eligibility.counterfactual: Removing the duplicated considerations would leave no separate basis for changing con burden completion.
